record.label: A minimizer has no terminal plateau or empty support
record.statement: For every admissible minimizer gamma, there do not exist 0<=a<1 and finite c>=0 with gamma=c on (a,1). Indeed the terminal defect yields q(t)-t<0 near 1 and hence G(s)<0 for s sufficiently close to 1, contradicting G>=0. In particular support cannot be empty, since that would force gamma=0.
record.boundary: Curated source-level mathematical statement, not an elaborated Lean extraction or independently accepted proof. Its displayed local hypotheses are quantified guards; a hypothetical plateau is not an added premise of the full-support theorem. Time 1 is outside the support domain; this route does not assume a contact point or derivative there. Includes c=0 and does not appeal to infinite support as an extra premise. The minimizer premise here belongs to the ordinary manuscript model; formal-interface hypotheses remain on the separate Lean target. This classification does not prove a transport between formal models.

aligned_passages.text: **Theorem 5.1 (full support).** In the pure zero-field SK model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimize $\mathcal P$. Then $\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1)$ and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing. For every associated diffusion started at zero, $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$ and $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ for $0\le t<1$. Keep the same minimiser, diffusion and moment function $q$ throughout. Section 3 has established $G\ge0$, $G=0$ on the support $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$, and the contact conditions $q(s)=s$, $q'(s)\le1$ at support points. At zero, the value identity comes from symmetry, and the slope bound requires $0\in S$. Section 4 supplies curvature on constant intervals for every admissible coefficient. These premises are available before any support gap is excluded. We first deal with the endpoint at one, then use the curvature estimate on the remaining intervals. For a terminal interval $(a,1)$, including empty support $[0,1)$, the cusp estimate gives $1-q(t)\gtrsim\sqrt{1-t}$ and hence $G<0$ near one. On a positive plateau with two contact endpoints, strict convexity puts $q'$ below its endpoint chord, although its integral must equal the interval length. On a zero plateau the heat argument makes $q'$ strictly increasing, below the right contact slope. At an initial gap, use the one-sided contact slope if $0\in S$; otherwise the coefficient is zero and symmetry supplies $q(0)=0$. **Why a terminal plateau violates the variational inequality.** Suppose that $\gamma=c$ on $(a,1)$, where $0\le a<1$ and $c\ge0$ is finite. The endpoint $1$ is outside the support domain, so there is no contact condition there to complete an endpoint-chord argument. Instead we will prove $$ 1-q(t)\ge C\sqrt{1-t} \tag{5.1} $$ for some $C>0$ and every $t$ sufficiently close to one. The proof separates two facts: the diffusion puts positive probability density near zero, and the smoothed terminal slope has a definite deficit from $\pm1$ in a shrinking window around zero. Fix $s\in(a,1)$ and let $\rho_s$ be the law of $X_s$. Choose $R<\infty$ such that $p_0=\rho_s([-R,R])>0$. For $c>0$, set $$ h(t,y)=\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt{1-t}Z|},\qquad \Phi(t,y)=c^{-1}\log h(t,y), $$ where $Z$ is standard normal. The drift on this interval is $c\Phi_x=h_x/h$, and the transition density is $$ k_{s,t}(x,y)=p_{t-s}(y-x)\frac{h(t,y)}{h(s,x)},\qquad p_v(z)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/(2v)}. \tag{5.2} $$ The heat-semigroup identity normalises this kernel; equivalently, for Brownian motion started at $(s,x)$, $h(t,B_t)/h(s,x)$ is the positive mean-one change of measure which adds the drift $h_x/h$. For $c=0$, the same kernel formula applies with $h=1$, and the value function is the ordinary heat evolution of $|x|$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, proof of (6.6)][fs-var]. Put $L=1-s$ and $\delta=L/2$. For $s+\delta\le t<1$, $|x|\le R$ and $|y|\le1$, $$ p_{t-s}(y-x)\ge (2\pi L)^{-1/2}e^{-(R+1)^2/(2\delta)}=:k_*>0, $$ while $h(t,y)\ge1$ and $h(s,x)\le e^{cR}\mathbb E e^{c\sqrt L|Z|}=:M<\infty$. Integrating (5.2) over the part of $\rho_s$ in $[-R,R]$ therefore gives a density $f_t$ of $X_t$ with $$ f_t(y)\ge p_0k_*/M=:m>0 \quad(s+\delta\le t<1,\ |y|\le1). \tag{5.3} $$ Only positive mass of a compact set was needed at time $s$; no density assumption on $\rho_s$ has entered. Now write $\varepsilon=1-t$ and restrict to $|y|\le\sqrt\varepsilon$. Differentiating the terminal heat formula gives, with the unweighted interpretation for $c=0$, $$ u(t,y)= \frac{\mathbb E[\operatorname{sgn}(y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z) e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}]} {\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}}. $$ The denominator is at most $D=e^c\mathbb E e^{c|Z|}<\infty$. Each sign has unnormalised mass at least $p_*:=\mathbb P(Z\ge1)>0$: the threshold $|y/\sqrt\varepsilon|$ is at most one, and the exponential weight is at least one. Hence each sign has tilted probability at least $\theta=p_*/D\in(0,1/2)$. It follows that $$ |u(t,y)|\le1-2\theta,\qquad 1-u(t,y)^2\ge4\theta(1-\theta)=:\kappa>0. $$ Multiplying this uniform deficit by the density lower bound (5.3) and the window width $2\sqrt\varepsilon$ yields $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,y)^2)f_t(y)\,dy \ge 2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ This proves (5.1) with $C=2m\kappa$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, density and terminal-window estimates][fs-var]. The sign of the contradiction is now explicit. For $s'$ sufficiently close to one, the estimate holds at every $t\in[s',1)$, so $$ \begin{aligned} G(s')&=\int_{s'}^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\\ &\le\frac{(1-s')^2}{2} -\frac{2C}{3}(1-s')^{3/2}<0. \end{aligned} $$ The final inequality holds once $\sqrt{1-s'}<4C/3$. It contradicts the nonnegative cost of adding an atom at $s'$. This proof covers $c=0$ as well as $c>0$. In particular, empty support is impossible: then $\mu_\gamma=0$ and $\gamma=0$ on all of $[0,1)$. Because $(0,b)$ contains no mass, the support condition at zero forces an atom there and hence $c=\gamma(0)>0$. Its absence has not been proved at this stage. **Lemma 2 (constant-interval curvature; [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][FS]).** Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, with its associated diffusion and moment $q$. If $\gamma=c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, called a plateau, then for $t\in I$ $$ q'''(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \quad\text{if }c>0. \tag{3} $$ If $c=0$, then $q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0$. Minimality is not a hypothesis of this lemma. Section 3 derives its moment polynomial and explains the integrated estimate imported from the source. **Proof of Theorem 1, assuming Lemma 2.** A complementary interval with two support endpoints admits two contact conditions; an initial interval without support at zero has coefficient zero; a terminal interval is handled here by a boundary estimate. Suppose $(\ell,r)$ is a support gap with endpoints in $S$ and $r<1$. The coefficient is a positive constant there: support at $\ell$ and absence of mass immediately to its right force $\mu_\gamma([0,\ell])>0$. Strict convexity of $q'$ and (2) give $$ q'(t)<\frac{r-t}{r-\ell}q'(\ell) +\frac{t-\ell}{r-\ell}q'(r)\leq1 \qquad(\ell0$, hence $q'(t)0$ and all $t$ sufficiently close to one. Two estimates produce this scale. The heat representation of the terminal value $|x|$ gives $1-u(t,x)^2\geq\kappa>0$ on $|x|\leq\sqrt{1-t}$. A transition-kernel comparison from a fixed earlier time gives a density $f_t(x)\geq m>0$ on the fixed window $|x|\leq1$, uniformly as $t\uparrow1$. Thus $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,x)^2)f_t(x)\,dx \geq2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ The time-uniform density estimate, proved in Lemma 6.3, equations (6.6)–(6.7), is essential; pointwise positivity of each density would not suffice.
